title: Application equipment for pest management interventions

lessons.title: Types of application equipment
lessons.html:
Matching equipment to the job

The right equipment puts the right amount of product on the target, with minimal waste and exposure. The wrong equipment wastes product, causes drift and contamination, and may make a treatment fail. Pest management officers must know the main types, how they work and when to use each.

Liquid sprayers

  • Compression (pressure) sprayers: hand-pumped tanks of a few litres to about 10 litres, used for crack and crevice, spot and general surface treatments indoors. Many have a pressure regulator to keep output constant.
  • Knapsack sprayers: carried on the back with a lever pump; widely used for weeds, invader plants and perimeter treatments.
  • Motorised and vehicle-mounted sprayers: pumps driven by an engine or electric motor, used for large areas, termite soil treatments and herbicide work along roads and fence lines.

Nozzles

The nozzle controls flow rate, droplet size and spray pattern. Fan nozzles give an even band for surfaces and weeds; cone nozzles give fine droplets for foliage; pin-stream nozzles place product into cracks and crevices. Coarser droplets reduce drift. Low-drift nozzles are preferred near sensitive areas.

Dusters and granule applicators

Hand bulb or bellows dusters push insecticide dust into wall voids, electrical conduits and other dry spaces. Granule spreaders apply granular products evenly.

Space treatment equipment

  • ULV (ultra-low-volume) cold foggers produce very fine droplets for flying insects in enclosed spaces.
  • Thermal foggers use heat to vaporise a carrier into a visible fog. They present fire risk and must never be used near ignition sources or in dusty grain environments without strict controls.

Bait application

Gel bait guns place precise dots of cockroach or ant gel. Tamper-resistant rodent bait stations hold bait securely. Both minimise exposure of people and non-target animals.

Fumigation equipment

Fumigation uses specialised equipment: gas-proof sheets, sand snakes for sealing, applicators or dispensers for fumigant-generating products, gas monitoring instruments and breathing apparatus. Only trained and registered fumigators may use it.

lessons.title: Calibration and correct operation
lessons.html:
Why calibrate?

The label gives a dose, such as an amount of product per 100 litres of water or per hectare or per square metre. To deliver that dose, you must know how much your equipment actually applies. Nozzles wear, pressures vary and walking speeds differ between operators. Calibration measures actual output so that you mix and apply correctly. Under-application causes control failure and resistance; over-application wastes money, raises risk and may exceed residue limits.

A simple calibration method for a knapsack or compression sprayer

  1. Fill the sprayer with clean water only.
  2. Mark out a test area, for example 10 m by 2 m, or a known length of band.
  3. Pump to the working pressure and spray the test area at your normal walking speed and nozzle height.
  4. Measure how much water was used by refilling to the original level with a measuring jug.
  5. Calculate the application volume per square metre or per hectare.
  6. Use this volume, with the label rate, to work out how much product goes into each tank.

Repeat the test two or three times and use the average. Calibrate whenever you change nozzles, pressure, operator or product type, and at regular intervals.

Checking flow rate of nozzles

Collect output from each nozzle for a fixed time, such as one minute, into a measuring jug. Replace any nozzle whose output differs significantly from the manufacturer's chart or from the others.

Correct operation

  • Read the equipment manual and the product label before use.
  • Inspect for leaks, cracked hoses, damaged seals and blocked filters before filling.
  • Mix in a safe area, with PPE, adding product to partially filled water as the label directs.
  • Maintain constant pressure, speed and nozzle height.
  • Do not spray in wind conditions that the label warns against.
  • Never blow out a blocked nozzle by mouth. Clean it with a soft brush or replace it.
  • Never leave pressurised equipment in the sun or unattended.

For space and fogging equipment, follow the manufacturer's settings for droplet size and output and ensure the area is evacuated and secured.

lessons.title: Cleaning, maintenance and storage of equipment
lessons.html:
After every job

Equipment that is not cleaned becomes a source of contamination. Herbicide residues left in a sprayer can damage plants on the next job; insecticide residues can contaminate food areas; corroded parts leak onto the operator.

Cleaning procedure

  1. Spray out any small remaining mix on the target area if the label allows; never dump excess into drains or water.
  2. Release pressure before opening the tank.
  3. Triple rinse the tank with clean water, spraying the rinse through the lance and nozzle onto a suitable treated area or into an approved rinsate collection system.
  4. Use a tank cleaner if the label of the previous product recommends it, especially after herbicides.
  5. Remove and clean nozzles, filters and screens with a soft brush.
  6. Wash the exterior of the equipment.
  7. Wear PPE throughout cleaning.

Maintenance

ComponentCheck
Hoses and sealsCracks, leaks, perishing rubber
Pump and pressure gaugeSmooth operation, accurate reading
NozzlesWear, damage, correct type, flow rate
FiltersClean and intact
Straps and tanksSecure, no cracks
Engines and foggersService per manual, fuel safety

Keep a maintenance log for each item of equipment, including calibration results and repairs. Remove faulty equipment from use and tag it until repaired.

Dedicated equipment

Many operators keep separate sprayers, clearly marked, for herbicides and for insecticides. This greatly reduces the risk of herbicide damage to plants or insecticide contamination where it is not wanted.

Storage and transport

Store clean, dry and depressurised equipment in a secure, ventilated area, away from food and living spaces. Secure equipment in vehicles so it cannot tip or leak, separate from the driver and passengers.

Key points

  • Choose equipment and nozzles that put the label dose on the target with minimal drift.
  • Calibrate with clean water to know actual output before calculating the mix.
  • Inspect equipment before use and never blow out a nozzle by mouth.
  • Triple rinse and clean after every job without contaminating drains or water.
  • Maintain, log, store and transport equipment securely; consider dedicated herbicide sprayers.
